In draft/08-detailed-description.md, delete the whole paragraph beginning "The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool" and ending "...puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act." 31	- **[critical] Detailed Description asserts the failure behaviour of restart-threshold, rate-of-change, attachment, battery and display signalling** (draft/08-detailed-description.md, paragraph beginning "This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at whi) - This paragraph states how other devices behave in failure - that a pump-restart device will run its pump past the release vacuum when the leak exceeds pump capacity, that a rate-based warning fires on a fast leak and stays silent on a slow one that has consumed the whole reserve, and what attachment, battery-state and display signals do and do not tell a user. 1	This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.
2	
3	A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.
4	
5	The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.
6	
7	The warning vacuum is a vacuum which the decaying vacuum reaches before the release vacuum, and not the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve is the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum while any signal it gives remains tied to the value at which the pump is restarted rather than to the grip that remains. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.

The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

1	In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.
2	
3	FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.
4	
5	FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.
6	
7	The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50.
8	
9	The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.
10	
11	FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.
12	
13	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.
14	
15	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.
16	
17	The warning vacuum is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve is the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.
18	
19	This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. A restart value is a value at which a pump is run again; it says nothing about how much grip is left, and a device that answers its crossing by running its pump will, when the leak is larger than the pump can make up, run the pump all the way past the release vacuum while any signal it gives remains tied to the value at which the pump is restarted rather than to the grip that remains. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what gives the activation of the warning indicator 32 the meaning that the grip is failing and that the user still has hold of the panel. It is also a different decision from warning on how fast the vacuum is changing: a warning given on rate fires on a fast leak whatever grip is left, and stays quiet on a slow leak that has nonetheless eaten the whole reserve. And it is a different decision from reporting that attachment has been achieved, or that the battery is charged, or that a measured value can be read off a display, none of which tells a user carrying a slab how much of the hold is left.
20	
21	The distinction matters more for a hand-carried tool than for equipment on a frame or a boom. Frame-mounted and suspended lifters can be given their own remedies for a failing grip: a second vacuum source, a reservoir, an interlock that refuses further motion. A cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has none of these. The only thing that can act on a failing grip is the person holding the handle 16, and a person needs to be told while there is still something to be done. Activating the warning indicator 32 while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load is what puts the warning inside the window in which the user can act.
22	
23	In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.
24	
25	A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.
26	
27	At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.
28	
29	The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.

The warning vacuum is a vacuum which the decaying vacuum reaches before the release vacuum, and not the vacuum at which a pump would be asked to run again. This is what makes the warning useful in a hand-held tool rather than merely informative. A frame-mounted or suspended lifter can respond to a failing grip by itself, by cutting in a second vacuum source or by refusing to move. A cordless handheld lifter has no such recourse: the only actuator available is the person holding the handle, and a person needs an interval in which to act. Because the decaying vacuum reaches the warning vacuum before it reaches the release vacuum, the interval is the time in which the grip that remains between those two vacuums is still holding the load.

In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, because of dust or grit under the lip, a textured or porous face, a damaged lip, or flexing of the workpiece 50, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost. From the point of view of the person holding the panel this loss is silent: nothing about the feel of the tool changes.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve is the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

This is a different design decision from choosing a vacuum at which to run a pump again. The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve is the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

input.summary: The request asks for the sheets to be finished automatically from the saved candidate, the geometry, semantic, OCR, sheet-number, leader, endpoint and independent-review checks to be run, and filing readiness published only once all pass. The gating check in front of all of those is the source-fidelity preflight, which failed on six items, so that is what this turn cleared. Three were figure-brief statements that carried technical substance rather than depiction convention: the FIG. 1 rigid body is no longer dimensioned by proportion, the FIG. 1 handle arch no longer carries a stated finger-clearance function, and the FIG. 2 port is no longer placed on the vertical centre line, in the bullet or in its anchor, so it now reads exactly as the location-neutral FIG. 3 wording does. Three were invention-text prose importing uncited prior-art characterisation: the summary sentences and the whole detailed-description paragraph about what frame-mounted and suspended lifters can do are gone, the detailed-description paragraph asserting how restart-threshold, rate-of-change, attachment, battery-state and display signalling behave in failure is gone, and the enumerated leak causes with the assertion that the failure is silent are reduced to the supported statement that an imperfect seal lets air bleed back so the vacuum is progressively lost. Deleting the summary sentences left "the interval" without an antecedent, so that clause now names the interval it means, running from activation of the warning indicator to arrival at the release vacuum, which is the same interval the detailed description already describes. The cited prior-art comparisons remain in the Background, where they belong. Numerals, sheet assignments, claims 1 to 7, the numeral table and the drawing descriptions are unchanged and in agreement, with all sixteen numerals on sheets and no sheet over eight. What I could not do is the rendering and publication the request also asks for: figure files in this workspace are Markdown specifications, image files are not mine to create, and the renderer, the numeral labeller and the audit-evidence generator run outside it, so the sheets and review/figure-audit-evidence.json still do not exist and filing readiness cannot be published from here.
reasoning: Every one of the six fixes was a deletion or a narrowing to disclosed wording. Nothing was added to the application text, no optional embodiment was introduced to fill a gap, and no numeral, claim limitation or figure assignment changed, so the invention is exactly what the reviewer's ledger traced to the inventor's passage.

The two FIG. 1 items were the clearest case of geometry doing technical work. A proportion tells a reader the body is squat rather than tall, which bears on where a pump can sit inside it, and finger clearance under the arch asserts how the hand engages the handle. The arch survives as a plain generic outline, which is all a part the inventor named but never drew is entitled to.

For the port I followed the FIG. 3 wording rather than inventing a third phrasing, because the port is a functional flow boundary: saying it sits on the vertical centre line asserts an on-axis flow path through the cup rather than an off-axis one through a side wall. Both briefs now say only that it is the opening through which the pump draws air, so the two sheets agree and neither fixes a location.

The two deleted detailed-description paragraphs were the passages a later prosecution argument would have been built from, which is why they had to go rather than be softened. An argument resting on uncited assertions about how other machines fail would not survive the first check against the references, and the Background already carries the same comparisons tied to US-10625955-B2, CN-110630621-B, US-10518985-B2, WO-2017156581-A1 and the rest. Nothing supported was lost, and no claim depended on those paragraphs.

The leak-cause list was reduced rather than removed entirely, because the fact that an imperfect seal lets air back in is what makes the warning function operate at all; what came out were the specific operating conditions and the sensory claim that the failure is silent, neither of which the inventor states.

One consequential edit beyond the six: with the surrounding sentences deleted, the summary's closing clause referred to an interval that no longer had an antecedent. Naming it as the interval from activation of the warning indicator to arrival at the release vacuum restores the antecedent using the detailed description's own words, and adds no matter.

I verified after the edits that all sixteen numerals still appear in the specification, in numerals.md and across the four sheets in the same distribution the reviewer recorded, that no claim term lacks description support beyond claim boilerplate, and that no drafting marker or em dash exists in draft/ or figures/.

figures/FIG-2-VERTICAL-SECTION-THROUGH-THE-LIFTER.md: the port bullet and the anchor for 22 no longer place the port on the vertical centre line, matching the FIG. 3 wording

draft/06-summary.md: the sentences asserting what frame-mounted and suspended lifters can do, and the pump-restart contrast preceding them, are deleted; the surviving sentence now names the interval it refers to, running from activation of the warning indicator to arrival at the release vacuum

Removing the comparative paragraphs from the invention text does not weaken that position, because the comparisons live in the Background with their citations: a suction plate assembly with a preset limit pressure and a malfunction alarm in US-5310232-A, high and low predetermined pressures for pump stop and restart with warning information transmitted to an external electronic device in US-10625955-B2, a restart on a second predetermined pressure in CN-110630621-B, a rate of vacuum change in US-10518985-B2, a preselected minimum and a preselected safe level in WO-2017156581-A1, a predetermined degree of vacuum in US-5184858-A, power-source charge sufficiency in US-5374090-A, a displayed negative pressure value in US-2024424646-A1, usage states in CN-2806399-Y, and module functional condition in WO-2022236379-A1. None of them fixes a threshold by reference to the vacuum still needed to hold the load, and that remains the ground the claims stand on.

3	Source-fidelity preflight v10 (functional-surface-geometry) on p6, "Cordless Handheld Vacuum Lifter With Grip-Loss Warning Indicator".

5	LEDGER - what traces cleanly. The inventor's authority is one USER passage (input/disclosure.md, repeated verbatim as the first USER turn of input/conversation.md) plus two corrective USER turns (remove "QA MARKER ONE"; begin the Background with "A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is used to"), neither of which adds technical matter. That passage affirmatively supports: cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100; rigid body 14 comprising handle 16; suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body and comprising flexible sealing lip 12; electric vacuum pump 20 disposed within the rigid body and configured to draw air through port 22 to create a vacuum; pressure sensor 30 monitoring the grip vacuum; warning indicator 32 driven by the sensor and activating when vacuum is lost; rechargeable battery 40 powering the pump; the indicator warning "before a load can be dropped"; and glass and stone panels as the workpiece 50. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass pane or a stone slab, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning vacuum is the vacuum which is reached, as the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50 is lost, before the release vacuum is reached. The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. Nothing in the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 has to intervene and nothing has to be fast, because the reserve is what buys the time, and the reserve is the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. input.summary: Two findings, both fixed by deletion or by aligning to wording the application already uses. The detailed-description sentence asserting that nothing in the lifter has to intervene and nothing has to be fast is deleted, so that paragraph now ends with the supported statement that during the interval running from activation of the warning indicator 32 to arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip. That removes the last residue of the comparative prior-art argument from the invention text and with it the negative form that could have read as a disclaimer of a lifter which answers a falling vacuum by running its pump. The FIG. 1 paragraph now calls the workpiece 50 a glass panel or a stone panel, the same designation used in the embodiment paragraph, the Summary, the Abstract and claims 4 and 7, so one part carries one exemplar name throughout the description and the claim terms read on the description directly. The Background's ordinary-language framing is left exactly as the user's instruction set it. Nothing else changed: claims 1 to 7, the numeral table, the drawing descriptions and all four figure briefs are untouched, all sixteen numerals still appear in the specification, in the table and across the four sheets in the same distribution, and no drafting marker or dangling antecedent remains.
reasoning: Both fixes were subtractive. The first removes an assertion about the claimed device's operating requirement and response speed that no inventor passage supports, and it costs nothing, because the two sentences before it already carry the supported content: the indicator activates while the cup is still retaining the load, and there is an interval in which the user still has a held load and a working grip.

Deleting that sentence also closes a scope hazard rather than opening one. Stated negatively, it read as a disclaimer of pump response during a decaying vacuum, which the inventor never made; with it gone the description says only what happens at the warning vacuum and leaves the pump's behaviour unconstrained.

The workpiece fix is a terminology alignment, not a change of meaning. The inventor's word is panels, the claims recite a glass panel or a stone panel, and the FIG. 1 paragraph was the only place still saying pane and slab, so aligning it removes an equivalence the reader would otherwise have had to supply between the claim term and the description.

I confirmed the deletion left no dangling reference: the paragraph's remaining sentences do not depend on the reserve clause that went with it, and the word reserve is still introduced and used earlier in the same paragraph, so nothing refers back to text that is no longer there.

After the edits I rechecked that the specification numeral set, the numeral table and the union of the four sheet lists are still identical at all sixteen numerals, that no claim term lacks description support beyond claim boilerplate, and that no drafting note or em dash exists anywhere in draft/ or figures/.

The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. 12	
13	The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.
14	
15	Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass panel or a stone panel, is gripped on its face by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the face of the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.

Two vacuums are of interest during that loss. One is the release vacuum, the vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load, that is, the vacuum at which the load can be dropped. The other is the warning vacuum, the vacuum at which the warning indicator 32 is driven to activate.

The warning indicator 32 accordingly activates at a moment when the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load, and the grip that remains between the warning vacuum and the release vacuum is a reserve. The warning indicator 32 is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. During the interval that runs from the activation of the warning indicator 32 to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, the user still has a held load and a working grip.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against a face of the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against a face of the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, as the vacuum is lost, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate at the warning vacuum, which is reached before the release vacuum at which the suction cup 10 ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator 32 is therefore activated while the suction cup 10 is still retaining the load.

This summary introduces a selection of concepts that are described further in the detailed description. It is not intended to identify essential features of the claimed subject matter, nor to limit the scope of the claims.

A cordless handheld vacuum lifter is disclosed. The lifter has a rigid body comprising a handle, and a suction cup carried by the rigid body. The suction cup comprises a flexible sealing lip which is placed against a workpiece. An electric vacuum pump is disposed within the rigid body and draws air through a port so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup and the workpiece, by which vacuum the suction cup grips the workpiece and retains a load. A pressure sensor monitors the vacuum. A warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor. A rechargeable battery powers the electric vacuum pump.

The warning indicator activates as the vacuum is lost. It does so at a warning vacuum which the vacuum reaches, as the vacuum is lost, before the vacuum reaches a release vacuum at which the suction cup ceases to retain the load. The warning indicator therefore activates while the suction cup is still retaining the load, and there is grip in reserve at the moment the user is told.

Because the decaying vacuum reaches the warning vacuum before it reaches the release vacuum, there is an interval, running from the activation of the warning indicator to the arrival of the vacuum at the release vacuum, in which the grip that remains between those two vacuums is still holding the load.

In embodiments, the warning indicator warns a user before the load can be dropped. In embodiments, the workpiece is a glass panel or a stone panel.

A method of lifting a workpiece with such a lifter is also disclosed. The method includes placing the flexible sealing lip against the workpiece, drawing air through the port with the electric vacuum pump to create the vacuum, carrying the load on the suction cup by the handle, monitoring the vacuum with the pressure sensor while the load is retained, and activating the warning indicator as the vacuum is lost, at the warning vacuum, that is, while the suction cup still retains the load and before the vacuum has reached the release vacuum.

# FIG. 4 - Flow diagram of the method of lifting a workpiece

**View type:** Flow diagram. Five plain rectangular boxes are arranged in a single vertical
column in the middle of the drawing area, with a plain arrow running from each box down to the
box below it. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the filing margins.

**What is shown**

The five boxes, from the top of the column to the bottom of the column, are the steps of the
method:

- The uppermost box is the placing step 202.
- The box immediately below the uppermost box is the evacuating step 204.
- The middle box is the carrying step 206.
- The box immediately above the lowest box is the monitoring step 208.
- The lowest box is the activating step 210.

A further plain arrow returns from the left side of the box of the monitoring step 208 upward
and back into the left side of that same box, showing that monitoring continues while the load
is retained.

The part names of the steps are semantic identifiers used to say which box each numeral
belongs to. They do not appear as drawing text, and no text is drawn inside the boxes.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass panel or a stone panel, is gripped by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the vacuum is lost, and is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate when the vacuum is lost.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

input.summary: All six findings are fixed. The two-level vacuum framework is out of the application entirely: claim 1's warning element now reads that the warning indicator is driven by the pressure sensor and configured to activate when the vacuum is lost, claim 5's final step reads that the warning indicator, driven by the pressure sensor, is activated when the vacuum is lost, and the Summary, Detailed Description and Abstract carry the same disclosed wording. With that framework gone, the reserve of grip and the timed interval go with it: Summary paragraphs 5 and 7 are replaced by the single sentence that the warning indicator activates when the vacuum is lost, and the two description paragraphs that named the release vacuum, the reserve and the interval are replaced by one sentence stating that the indicator activates when the vacuum is lost and is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped. Claims 2 and 6, which recite warning before the load can be dropped, are untouched, so the disclosed timing statement is still claimed. In the briefs, the handle is now a plain generic grip outline on the rigid body 14 in FIG. 1 and an unnumbered unsectioned outline beyond the cut walls in FIG. 2, with no cut-topology statement; the attitude and side wording is gone from FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, so the cup is carried by the rigid body 14 and the workpiece 50 is a flat broken-off slab in contact with the lip, with no underside, upper face, below or horizontal; and the FIG. 4 self-return arrow and its continuous-monitoring statement are deleted, leaving the five boxes joined by the four downward arrows. "A face of" is gone from claim 3, claim 5's first step and the three description paragraphs, which also aligns claim 5 with the Summary. All sixteen numerals still appear in the specification, in numerals.md and across the four sheets in the same distribution, no sheet carries more than eight, and no claim term lacks description support.
reasoning: The warning-vacuum and release-vacuum recitation was the feature that carried claim 1 away from US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, so removing it costs the independent claims their distinguishing limitation. I removed it anyway and did not substitute anything in its place, because source fidelity governs: the finding is that no USER passage names a release vacuum or orders two levels, and inventing a replacement distinction would repeat the error rather than cure it. What remains in the independent claims is the disclosed function, the indicator activating when the vacuum is lost, with the before-a-drop timing kept in dependent claims 2 and 6 where the disclosure puts it.

Deleting the two-level framework made the reserve and interval sentences unsupportable on their own terms as well as untraced, so both went in the same pass. I checked afterwards that nothing else refers back to them: the words release vacuum, warning vacuum, reserve and interval now appear nowhere in draft/ or figures/.

For the handle I used the reviewer's replacement wording verbatim in both briefs rather than choosing a different generic form, and I added nothing to the specification to justify the visual choice. The FIG. 2 sentence now says only that the handle is not sectioned and appears as a plain unnumbered outline beyond the cut walls, which removes the cut-topology assertion without leaving the section incomplete. Numeral 16 stays on FIG. 1, so the numeral table is unaffected.

The attitude fix touched three briefs. FIG. 1's view type no longer says the lifter grips the upper face, its cup bullet no longer says joined to the underside or below the body, its slab is no longer horizontal, and the anchors for 12 and the cutting-plane endpoints are reworded to match. FIG. 2's cup is carried by the rigid body with its open side facing the workpiece, which states the relationship the section needs without fixing which side of the body carries it. FIG. 3's cup is in contact with the slab rather than seated on its upper face. The break-line convention and the page arrangement are retained, as directed.

The FIG. 4 loop was the only place the method was said to monitor continuously. Removing the arrow and its explanatory sentence leaves the diagram showing exactly the five disclosed acts in sequence, which is what the claims and description recite.

Deleting a face of in five places also removed the mismatch between claim 5's first step and the Summary, which already recited placing the lip against the workpiece. Claim 3 keeps its panel limitation, so it still adds something claim 1 does not carry.

After the edits I verified that the specification numeral set, numerals.md and the union of the four sheet lists remain identical at all sixteen numerals, that no claim word is missing from the description beyond claim boilerplate, that no drafting marker or em dash survives, and that no paragraph left a dangling antecedent.

The nearest references remain US-10625955-B2 and CN-110630621-B, which disclose an electric suction lifter with a main body and handle, a pump, a pressure sensing unit, a rechargeable battery and a warning unit, so the distinguishing weight now rests on the dependent claims that recite the disclosed timing, claims 2 and 6, warning a user before the load can be dropped, and on claims 3, 4 and 7 for the panel workpiece. In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass panel or a stone panel, is gripped by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. The warning indicator 32 activates when the vacuum is lost, and is in this way configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

input.summary: Three fixes, each confined to the file the finding named. The FIG. 2 brief now says that where the cutting plane meets the handle, the handle is shown as a single cut region above the upper wall of the shell, cross-hatched and unnumbered, so the section is executable as a true section on line 2-2 of FIG. 1: the FIG. 1 plane is centred on the handle and must cut it, and FIG. 2 no longer directs that the handle be drawn uncut and outside the cut walls. The FIG. 1 brief, the numeral table and all specification text are untouched, and the handle keeps numeral 16 on FIG. 1 only. In the detailed description, the causal connective is gone: the paragraph now states the two disclosed facts side by side, that the warning indicator 32 activates when the vacuum is lost and that the warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped, which is the wording claims 2 and 5 already use. Claim 3 reciting the unsupported genus "a panel" is cancelled and the set renumbered, so the claims now run 1 to 6: apparatus claim 1, the before-a-drop warning as claim 2, the glass or stone panel as claim 3, the method as claim 4, and the two method dependents as claims 5 and 6 with their dependencies updated to claim 4. Nothing supported was lost, since the disclosed species is still claimed in claims 3 and 6, and the placement of the lip against the workpiece remains in claim 1 and in the first step of claim 4. All sixteen numerals still appear in the specification, in numerals.md and across the four sheets in the same distribution, with FIG. 1 carrying 10, 12, 14, 16, 50, 100; FIG. 2 carrying 10, 12, 14, 20, 22, 50; FIG. 3 carrying 10, 20, 22, 30, 32, 40, 50; and FIG. 4 carrying 202 to 210.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 fix resolves the conflict in favour of the source view, which is the right direction: FIG. 1 defines the cutting plane, its alignment on the lifter's centre line, both endpoints and both arrow directions, and a section brief cannot contradict the plane it is taken on. The cut region stays unnumbered, so numeral 16 remains carried only by FIG. 1 and the sheet-to-numeral assignment is unchanged.

The connective fix restores the disclosure's own structure. The inventor states two things without linking them, so the description now states them the same way, in two sentences. This also removes the awkward reading in which a vacuum already lost is treated as the state that precedes the load being dropped.

Cancelling claim 3 costs nothing in coverage. Its genus had no matching description passage, since the summary and description both give only a glass panel or a stone panel, and its second clause repeated the placement of the lip against the workpiece that claim 1 already recites. The disclosed species survives as claim 3 for the apparatus and claim 6 for the method.

Renumbering was done in full: the method claim is now claim 4, and both method dependents were repointed to claim 4 rather than left referring to a claim number that no longer designates the method. I checked the numbering runs 1 to 6 with no gap and no dangling dependency.

After the edits I verified that the specification numeral set, numerals.md and the union of the four sheet lists remain identical at all sixteen numerals, that no claim word lacks description support beyond claim boilerplate, and that no drafting marker or em dash survives in draft/ or figures/.

In the following description, reference is made to the accompanying drawings, which form a part hereof and in which are shown by way of illustration specific embodiments. Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

FIG. 1 shows a cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 in use. The cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 comprises a rigid body 14 comprising a handle 16, and a suction cup 10 carried by the rigid body 14. The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass panel or a stone panel, is gripped by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. The pressure of the surrounding atmosphere acting on the outside of the suction cup 10 then clamps the suction cup 10, and with it the rigid body 14 and the handle 16, to the workpiece 50, so that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. Running the electric vacuum pump 20 draws further air through the port 22 and increases the vacuum; air leaking back is a loss of vacuum and a weakening of the grip.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum. If the seal between the flexible sealing lip 12 and the workpiece 50 is imperfect, air bleeds back and the vacuum is progressively lost.

The warning indicator 32 activates when the vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate when the vacuum is lost.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. Features described in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another unless the combination is technically impossible. Terms such as upper, lower, above, and below are used with reference to the orientation shown in the drawings and do not restrict the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 to any particular attitude in use. The scope of protection is defined by the claims.

Other embodiments may be used and structural changes may be made without departing from the scope of the disclosure. Like numerals refer to like parts throughout.

The suction cup 10 comprises a flexible sealing lip 12. A workpiece 50, such as a glass panel or a stone panel, is gripped by the suction cup 10 and is carried by the user by way of the handle 16.

FIG. 2 is a vertical section through the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100, showing the suction cup 10, the flexible sealing lip 12, the rigid body 14, an electric vacuum pump 20, a port 22, and the workpiece 50.

The suction cup 10 carries the flexible sealing lip 12. The flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50.

The electric vacuum pump 20 is disposed within the rigid body 14. The electric vacuum pump 20 is configured to draw air through the port 22 so as to create a vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. A load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

FIG. 3 shows the arrangement schematically. A pressure sensor 30 is configured to monitor the vacuum. A warning indicator 32 is driven by the pressure sensor 30. A rechargeable battery 40 is configured to power the electric vacuum pump 20. The electric vacuum pump 20 draws air through the port 22 from between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50.

The warning function operates as follows. The electric vacuum pump 20 creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.
The warning indicator 32 activates when the vacuum is lost. The warning indicator 32 is configured to warn a user before the load can be dropped.

In embodiments, the workpiece 50 is a glass panel or a stone panel, the flexible sealing lip 12 being placed against the panel. Such a panel is the workpiece 50 for which the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is principally intended.

A method of lifting a workpiece 50 with the cordless handheld vacuum lifter 100 is shown in FIG. 4. At a placing step 202, the flexible sealing lip 12 is placed against the workpiece 50. At an evacuating step 204, the electric vacuum pump 20, powered by the rechargeable battery 40, draws air through the port 22 and creates the vacuum between the suction cup 10 and the workpiece 50. At a carrying step 206, the workpiece 50 is lifted and a load is carried on the suction cup 10 by the handle 16, the load being retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum.

At a monitoring step 208, the pressure sensor 30 monitors the vacuum while the load is retained. At an activating step 210, the pressure sensor 30 drives the warning indicator 32 to activate when the vacuum is lost.

The embodiments described above are illustrative rather than limiting. input.summary: All five findings are fixed, each by deletion or by the narrowing the review specified. In the detailed description, the atmospheric-clamping explanation and its load path through the rigid body 14 and handle 16 are replaced by the single supported sentence that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum, which is the wording claim 1, the method claim, the summary and the abstract already use; the sentence asserting that running the pump increases the vacuum and that leak-back weakens the grip is deleted in full; and the sentence supplying a cause and progression for the loss of vacuum, an imperfect lip seal with air bleeding back and a progressive decay, is deleted in full, so the warning paragraph now states only that the pump creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum, followed by the supported activation paragraph. In the briefs, the FIG. 2 handle bullet no longer fixes how many times the plane meets the handle or where the handle sits relative to the shell: it now says that where the cutting plane meets the handle, the handle is shown cut, cross-hatched and unnumbered, in agreement with the generic grip outline of FIG. 1. The FIG. 1 slab bullet no longer says the panel extends past both sides of the lifter and relies on the break lines alone to show indeterminate extent. Nothing else changed: claims 1 to 6, numerals.md, the Brief Description of the Drawings, the Summary, the Abstract and the FIG. 3 and FIG. 4 briefs are untouched, all sixteen numerals still appear in the specification, in the numeral table and across the four sheets in the same distribution, and no sheet carries more than eight.
reasoning: Every fix was subtractive, so no claim lost support and none needed amendment. The three description sentences that went were explanation the drafter had supplied around the disclosed facts, and what replaced them, that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum, is the exact phrase already used in the claims, the summary and the abstract, so the description still reads on every claim term.

For FIG. 2 I used the reviewer's replacement wording rather than devising my own, because the defect was precisely that any count or position I chose would be an assertion. Saying only that the handle is shown cut where the plane meets it leaves the topology to the generic grip outline FIG. 1 already establishes, keeps the section a true section on line 2-2, and keeps the cut region unnumbered so FIG. 2's coverage of 10, 12, 14, 20, 22 and 50 is unchanged.

The FIG. 1 slab bullet now carries only the break-line convention, which discharges the drawing's need to show indeterminate extent without fixing the panel as larger than the tool. The anchor for 50 was left as it was, since placing the numeral to the right of the suction cup is page placement rather than a size relationship.

Deleting the leak sentence closed up the paragraph break between the warning-function paragraph and the activation paragraph, so I restored the blank line. That is formatting only; no wording changed.

After the edits I confirmed the specification numeral set, numerals.md and the union of the four sheet lists are still identical at all sixteen numerals, that no claim word is missing from the description beyond claim boilerplate, and that no drafting marker or em dash survives in draft/ or figures/.

In the detailed description, the atmospheric-clamping explanation and its load path through the rigid body 14 and handle 16 are replaced by the single supported sentence that a load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum, which is the wording claim 1, the method claim, the summary and the abstract already use; the sentence asserting that running the pump increases the vacuum and that leak-back weakens the grip is deleted in full; and the sentence supplying a cause and progression for the loss of vacuum, an imperfect lip seal with air bleeding back and a progressive decay, is deleted in full, so the warning paragraph now states only that the pump creates the vacuum, the user lifts and carries the workpiece 50, and the load is retained on the suction cup 10 by the vacuum, followed by the supported activation paragraph. In the briefs, the FIG. 2 handle bullet no longer fixes how many times the plane meets the handle or where the handle sits relative to the shell: it now says that where the cutting plane meets the handle, the handle is shown cut, cross-hatched and unnumbered, in agreement with the generic grip outline of FIG. 1. reasoning: Every fix was subtractive, so no claim lost support and none needed amendment. The anchor for 50 was left as it was, since placing the numeral to the right of the suction cup is page placement rather than a size relationship.

Deleting the leak sentence closed up the paragraph break between the warning-function paragraph and the activation paragraph, so I restored the blank line. That is formatting only; no wording changed.
